common_name: Kidd's Orange Red Apple (Cox's Orange Pippin x Delicious, Parent of Gala)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with good air circulation, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Kidd's Orange Red was raised in New Zealand in the 1920s by orchardist J.H. Kidd from a cross of Cox's Orange Pippin and a red-skinned Delicious parent, inheriting the rich, aromatic, sweet-tart flavor of its Cox parent on a somewhat more reliably productive tree. It is best known today as one of the two parents of Gala, passing on its flavor heritage and red-flushed skin to that far more widely grown modern apple. Fruit is medium-sized with an orange-red flush over a yellow-green background and crisp, juicy, well-balanced flesh, ripening in early-to-mid fall and keeping reasonably well in cool storage for a few months. Give it a compatible pollinator and the same moderate winter chill and well-drained soil that Cox's Orange Pippin requires, since Kidd's Orange Red shares much of that parent's demanding, disease-prone nature in humid climates.

common_name: Wyken Pippin Apple (Old English Dessert and Cider Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Wyken Pippin is an old English dessert apple that originated in the eighteenth century at Wyken, near Coventry in Warwickshire, and it has stayed relevant largely through its role as a parent of later English apples, including Laxton's Superb. The medium, yellow-green fruit is lightly russeted and carries a firm, mild, sweet flavor considerably less sharp than many old English apples, making it a pleasant fresh-eating variety as well as a useful cider component. It ripens in mid-to-late fall and keeps reasonably well into winter in cool storage, a trait valued long before mechanical refrigeration existed. The tree is a dependable, moderately vigorous grower; provide a compatible pollinator and well-drained soil, since like most old heirloom apples it was never bred for scab or fire blight resistance in humid growing regions.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Purple Pony blooms very early in spring, often in February in zones 7-9, just before the reddish-purple foliage emerges.

directions: Purple Pony is a purple-leaf plum cultivar grown for the same rich burgundy-purple foliage and very early single pink flowers that define the group, opening before or alongside the emerging leaves in late winter to earliest spring. Like its better-known relatives Thundercloud and Krauter Vesuvius, it holds its dark foliage color through most of the growing season before fading somewhat by fall, and produces small, sparse, edible reddish plums that are secondary to its ornamental value. Plant it in full sun and well-drained soil as a small flowering accent or specimen tree, expecting the same fast early growth and relatively short 15- to 25-year lifespan typical of purple-leaf plum selections. Water regularly through the first year or two of establishment, then rely mainly on rainfall except during extended drought, and prune lightly after bloom to remove crossing or damaged branches.
